tagline: Hill farms and river valleys, with a trolley bridge turned flower garden.
intro: Route 112 runs from the Vermont border at Colrain to Huntington through open farmland, rolling hills, deep forests and small town centers. Western Massachusetts Scenic Byways presents the scenic route as a leisurely drive through working countryside. Farms along it produce apples, berries, squash, pumpkins, Christmas trees and maple syrup; some roadside tables sell on the honor system.

The highway acquired its present reach in stages. In 1930, Route 112 ended at Route 2, the Mohawk Trail, and used a more easterly alignment between Worthington and Cummington. The extension to Vermont followed former Route 56 in 1939. Another change came between 1966 and 1969, when an existing road between Goshen and Route 116 was upgraded and took over as Route 112.

Driving south, follow the North River through Colrain toward Shelburne Falls and its Bridge of Flowers. Continue through Buckland and Ashfield to Goshen, then turn west with Route 9 through Cummington before heading south through Worthington to Huntington. The East Branch of the Westfield River parallels much of the byway’s southern half.

moments.title: Colrain
moments.text: Colrain’s main road follows the North River, first beside its East Branch and then beside the joined stream toward Shelburne. The town has nine historic village areas, including Catamount Hill and the center called Colrain City. That city name began as a mid-nineteenth-century joke about the small village at the foot of Chandler Hill. Up in Catamount, a different distinction dates to May 1812: Colrain became the first town in the United States to fly the U.S. flag above a public schoolhouse.

moments.title: Bridge of Flowers
moments.text: A water main helped save the trolley bridge between Shelburne and Buckland. The Shelburne Falls and Colrain Street Railway built the concrete crossing in 1908 to carry freight connections to Colrain. Trucks took more of that work, and the railway went bankrupt in 1927. Antoinette Burnham proposed making the unused bridge a garden. Eighty loads of loam arrived in 1929. Its flowers range from April tulips to October chrysanthemums, a planted crossing where trolley freight once traveled.

moments.title: William Cullen Bryant Homestead
moments.text: William Cullen Bryant returned to his childhood home as a buyer and a builder. His grandfather built the hillside house in 1783, above the Westfield River valley. Bryant lived here from age four until he was 22; the property left the family in 1835. When he bought it back in 1865, he raised the original building and inserted a new first floor beneath it. The grounds also connect to his writing: the Rivulet Trail passes maple sugar bushes, old-growth hemlock and the stream described in his 1823 poem “The Rivulet.”
